title: A Year Ago, Aamir Khan Said No to Prime Video's 120 Crore. Sitaare Zameen Par Turned One, and the Gamble Looks Like Genius.
excerpt: Most stars take the OTT cheque and run. Mr. Perfectionist walked away from a fortune, sent his film to theatres only, then to YouTube pay-per-view, and dared the audience to come to him. They did — to the tune of 250 crore.
body:
Picture the meeting. A streaming executive slides a number across the table. One hundred and twenty crore, for the digital rights to a feel-good sports drama about a cynical basketball coach and ten differently-abled kids. It is the kind of offer most producers would sign before the coffee cooled. Aamir Khan looked at it, by every account, and said no.

A year later, Sitaare Zameen Par has just turned one, and that no is starting to look less like stubbornness and more like the smartest call in the room. The film grossed over 250 crore. And it did it the old way, with bodies in seats, not a paywall and an autoplay countdown.

An extraordinary 5-year journey with one of the most brilliant and loving Stars, Actors, Producers and Support Systems. You are an addiction for sure. — director R.S. Prasanna

That tribute landed on the anniversary, Saturday, as director R.S. Prasanna posted a photo with the Lagaan actor and called working with him "an addiction." It is a warm note, but the real story is the bet underneath it. When Sitaare Zameen Par released on June 20 last year, Khan did something the industry treated as borderline reckless: he refused to sell it to a streaming platform at all. No Netflix, no Prime, no eight-week window. Theatres, full stop. Later, he experimented with a pay-per-view model on YouTube before finally letting it land on SonyLIV nine months on.

For a man whose last outing, Laal Singh Chaddha, was a painful box-office failure in 2022, this was not a small risk. It was an act of faith, both in the film and in the idea that audiences will still leave the house for something that moves them. "I always wanted an OTT release," Khan clarified later, "but not so quickly after the theatre release." Translation: the cinema deserves the first dance.

The film itself was built to earn that faith. A spiritual successor to his 2007 landmark Taare Zameen Par and an official remake of the Spanish Campeones, it flipped the emotional register of the original. Where Taare made you cry, this one made you laugh. Khan plays Gulshan Arora, a suspended, rude, politically incorrect coach ordered into community service training a basketball team of players with disabilities. Genelia Deshmukh leads opposite him, and ten genuine newcomers, Aroush Datta, Gopi Krishna Varma, Samvit Desai and seven others, were cast in roles that asked them to simply be themselves on a giant screen. Shankar-Ehsaan-Loy scored it.

The diaspora played its part too. Sitaare Zameen Par cleared the British censors with a 12A and ran in cinemas worldwide, the kind of warm, multi-generational watch that gets a whole NRI family into a Saturday matinee in Jersey City or Hounslow. It is exactly the sort of film that streaming math tends to undervalue and a packed hall tends to reward.

What makes the anniversary worth marking is what it says about where Khan is headed. At 60-plus, with a third wedding to longtime partner Gauri Spratt on the horizon and a long-rumoured reunion with Rajkumar Hirani circling, he is once again the rare megastar willing to treat distribution as an artistic choice rather than an accounting one. He is also slated for a special appearance in Lokesh Kanagaraj's Coolie alongside Rajinikanth.

The lesson the trade should take, and probably won't, is that the OTT cheque is not always the ceiling. Sometimes it is the floor you trip over on your way to something bigger. Aamir Khan walked past 120 crore on principle and the audience handed him double on trust. A year on, the gamble reads as gospel. Mr. Perfectionist, it turns out, was right about the imperfect, beautiful, irreplaceable business of getting people to show up.
